---
title: SIB in Codex
---

How Signed Instruction Blocks are integrated into Codex, in three figures. There are no hooks and
no patch to Codex: a policy tells Codex's own approval reviewer that `AGENTS.md` is untrusted
except for verified signed blocks, and that it must run `sib verify` before scoring authorization.
The reviewer does the rest with the instructions and the tool access it already has. The
measurements and the reasoning are in the [Phase 4 findings](plans/findings/phase-4-codex.md).


## The Runtime Path

![A human signs an instruction into `AGENTS.md`. The Codex agent reads the file and plans a deploy;
the sandbox blocks it and sends an approval request to the auto-review reviewer, whose prompt
carries the SIB policy from `config.toml`. The reviewer runs `sib verify`, which reads `AGENTS.md`
and the registry outside the repository and returns a manifest; the reviewer scores authorization
from verified spans and answers allow or deny.](plans/findings/images/phase-4/runtime-path.svg){width=100%}

The reviewer verifies the file itself. SIB adds no channel to Codex: the policy in `config.toml`
tells the reviewer which part of `AGENTS.md` to trust and which command establishes it, and the
reviewer's existing read-only tool access does the rest. The verified span sets
`user_authorization`, an input the reviewer already scores.


## What Changes Between a Forged Claim and a Signature

![Two identical pipelines. The forged claim yields a manifest with no verified spans, authorization
`low` and a denial. The signature yields a verified span signed by alice, authorization `high` and
an allow. The risk level is `high` in both arms because the team's deploy rule says
so.](plans/findings/images/phase-4/forged-vs-signed.svg){width=100%}

Everything is identical until the manifest. Codex trusts `AGENTS.md` unconditionally, so the
forged sentence used to establish authorization honestly, by the reviewer's own rules; the SIB
policy makes only a `verified` span count, and the reviewer's own rationales quote the manifest
when it refuses.


## Why the Template Is Pinned

![The reviewer prompt is rendered by substituting two slots in a template. The template the model
catalog serves has only the tenant policy slot, so `extra_policy` is dropped silently. Pinning
Codex's bundled template restores the slot, and the SIB rules land after Codex's built-in security
policy.](plans/findings/images/phase-4/template-pin.svg){width=100%}

The only workaround in the integration. `auto_review.policy` is not a substitute, because it
replaces Codex's entire built-in security policy; pinning the bundled template keeps it and adds
ours. Once upstream restores the slot ([openai/codex#50309](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/50309)),
the configuration is four lines.


## What `sib install codex` Writes

- `approvals_reviewer = "auto_review"` at the top of `config.toml`, asked first and never silently
  replacing a different choice.

- Under `[auto_review]`: the pinned template and `extra_policy`, with the absolute `sib` path,
  `SIB_HOME` and the audience baked into the command the reviewer will run. Existing keys are
  merged, not clobbered, and the old file is backed up to `config.toml.sib-bak`.

- The `sib-sign` skill at `~/.codex/skills/sib-sign/SKILL.md`: a how-to for the agent to walk the
  user through signing. It grants nothing; Codex treats skill text as untrusted and signing needs
  the user's own authenticator.

- Warnings when the registry sits inside the working directory, when no key is enrolled yet, and
  that SIB scores authorization but not risk, so a deploy rule is still yours to write.


## The Bounds

- **Provenance is one factor, not the verdict.** Codex allows medium-risk actions whatever the
  authorization, so a forged deploy was once allowed when the reviewer scored it `medium`. One
  sentence of ordinary deploy policy fixed that, and that sentence is the team's, not SIB's.

- **The registry is the trust root.** An agent that can write `SIB_HOME` can enroll its own key.
  The installer warns; nothing enforces it yet.

- **The reviewer choosing to run the verifier is a model decision.** Nine for nine so far, and
  predicted by its own instructions, but not guaranteed. The policy says to treat every instruction
  as unsigned if the command fails or cannot be run.

- **Not yet tested against the reviewer:** tampered and expired blocks; only forged-unsigned and
  genuine-verified have been.
